#8887. The 3 Types of Running Workouts You Need to Train for Your First Half Marathon

These key weekly sessions will carry you to the finish line.

Nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon. As a beginner, 13.1 miles is an awesome way to approach long-distance running. You just need a plan that meets you where you’re at right now and progresses gradually to get you to the starting line feeling strong.

Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon plan created by Meg Takacs, CPT, a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.

It balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances. You’ll spread these workouts throughout 20 weeks, which gives you plenty of time to build rather than your typical 10- or 14-week plan.

Each workout progresses as you move through the plan, so it’s a good idea to familiarize yourself with their basic structure and purpose before you jump into training. Here’s how to get the most out of each workout.

Run/walks help you build aerobic fitness and endurance gradually. You’ll start with a one-minute run followed by a one-minute walk for 20 minutes total, adding one minute to the run interval every session. With run/walks starting at three times a week, you’ll work up to a 10-mile run/walk in week 16, where you run for 20-minute intervals and walk for two minutes (this is your weekend long run).

Do the run intervals at a comfortable, low-intensity pace, meaning you should be able to hold a conversation with a friend the whole time. On a scale of 1 to 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), aim for a 2 to 4 for effort level, with 1 being easy like a walk and 10 meaning all-out effort.

Why it works: This is the backbone of the beginner half marathon plan. Run/walk sessions help you build the endurance you need to run farther.

10 x 1 minute walk, 1 minute easy-effort run

In week four of this plan, you’ll start incorporating continuous easy runs, beginning with 25 minutes at a truly easy effort. The longest continuous run you will complete is 8 miles with as few walk breaks as possible by week 17.

Throughout the plan, there’s more of a focus on time-based easy runs rather than distance. “For beginners, time on your feet is more important than mileage in order to get your body gradually acclimated to running,” Takacs previously told Runner’s World.

Why it works: Continuous easy runs help boost endurance and give you the confidence you need to run farther.

Run 25 minutes at an easy effort (RPE 2 to 4), limiting walk breaks as much as possible.

The first of your weekly speed workouts begins in week 3. You’ll complete 400-meter repeats at a moderate effort with two-minute walks in between. Moderate effort is slightly above your easy effort, reaching a 4 to 6 out of 10 RPE. “The goal is to try and run each repeat faster than the last,” Takacs adds.

You should still be able to speak during the work intervals, but you’re breathing heavier and can only talk in phrases. Over the course of the training plan, you’ll work your way up to longer intervals, like 800-meter, 1200-meter, and mile repeats.

Why it works: Speed workouts aren’t just there to help you get faster; they also boost your overall fitness and running economy so easy runs feel easier.

Short postrun strides help build speed and leg turnover, and you’ll find them sprinkled throughout your plan. These accelerations will help you build more speed, improve your running form by getting your legs to turn over quicker, and boost your confidence.

The goal of strides is to run at a hard effort for 10 to 15 seconds, but it doesn’t have to be an all-out sprint. Aim for a 7 to 10 RPE; you should only be able to say a word or three at a time.

In any training plan, strength workouts are crucial to prevent injury, support your running economy and durability, and get stronger. In this plan, you’ll complete strength workouts once or twice a week before or after your runs. Depending on your preference, you can decide to run in the morning, then follow with strength in the afternoon or evening (or vice versa).

Takacs recommends starting with bodyweight exercises if you’re new to strength training and then adding in weights as you get stronger.

There’s a reason coaches tell runners to work hard and recover harder. Your recovery days are meant to feel like a true recovery where you can come back to your next run feeling refreshed, strong, and excited to get back out there.

It’s a good idea to loosen stiff muscles with foam rolling, stretching, and some mobility drills. If you need a complete day off, it’s also okay to not do anything at all except watch TV, read a book, or hang out with friends. A day off is good for the mind and the body. This is also a good opportunity to make sure you’re getting to bed early so you can show up to each run as your best, well-rested self.

With big savings from brands, now is a great time to score a deal to get some rides in before the snow starts falling!

No matter your budget or riding needs—from commuters to mountain bikers, experienced cyclists and brand-new riders—there is an e-bike for everyone and every age. Our test team rides dozens of electric bikes each year, and these are some of our favorites and the best deals out there right now.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. The Level platform has proven to be reliable, low-maintenance, and fun to ride—and it doesn’t break the bank.

The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. The bike also has regenerative braking, upping the range to 75 miles. For commutes and running errands, the Level comes standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Riders will also find the Level’s connected features very useful. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

Compared with earlier Aventure versions, the third-generation model rides smoother and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found previous models had too much torque, but Aventure fixed that issue. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-road, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths. However, the bike is burly; its weight and components limit its fun on technical singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price.

Aventon’s Pace 5 REC is a zippy e-bike that’s perfect for weekend cruises around town, the bike path, or even occasional commutes. The brand refined the Pace with a slew of updates, making it one of the best bang-for-your-buck step-throughs on the market. These include connected features (such as GPS tracking and theft deterrence), a powerful 750 Watt motor, regenerative braking, and an impressive 75-mile range. It’s offered in five colors (grey, mint, pink, orange, and teal) and two frame sizes.

The Pace 5 does not come with a rack, fenders, or a suspension fork. If you commute by bike frequently or use your e-bike for running errands, consider paying $200 more for the Level 4.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have much mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike tech, but it helps you get out and enjoy some rides without busting your budget.

The Cityscape stands out for its combination of low price, practical features (like a rack and fenders), and a UL-certified battery. Unlike some Amazon brands, Heybike offers a U.S. support line for warranty service or product questions.

Includes FREE accessories: Fast Charger, Running Boards, Frame Bag, Cushions, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Seat, and Orbitor.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Discounted to $1,699, the dual-battery model has up to 120 miles of range and a 28 mph top speed. A single-battery version is also available for $1,399; it boasts an impressive 60-mile range. Need even more battery power? The $1,999 Long Range model goes up to 170 miles from a single charge.

These prices make the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes on the market. And they’re a solid option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike. “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers and the Essentials package, I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Water-Resistant Panniers, Lock, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Saddle, Phone Mount, and Mirrors.

If you want power and range in a small package, the XP4 750 is right for you. It’s a fast, zippy Class 3 e-bike (pedal assist up to 28 mph) with a 330-pound payload capacity. To increase the XP4’s function and fun, the 750 has a 1310-watt peak motor output (200 watts more than the standard model) and an 85-mile range.

Whether you’re riding city streets on your commute or out for a weekend ride, this bike is fast, easy to ride, and a blast to pedal.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Fenders, Headlight, and Seatpost.

The XP Lite 2.0 scales back the XP4 750’s top speed and power, with pedal assist topping out at 20 mph, a peak motor output of 819 watts, and a reduced payload capacity of 275 pounds. It also drops the suspension fork found on the XP4, but still delivers an impressive range of up to 80 miles.

However, the XP Lite isn’t simply a stripped-down version of the XP4; it has some major advantages. At 49 pounds (without accessories and options), it’s 26 pounds lighter than the higher-powered model. This makes the Lite much easier to lift and transport. Plus, instead of an 8-speed drivetrain, the XP Lite features a low-maintenance Gates belt drive. That means no greasy chain, no finicky gear adjustments, and a quieter, cleaner ride. Yes, it’s a singlespeed, but the pedal-assist motor easily compensates for all but the steepest hills or heaviest loads.

Includes FREE accessories: Support Seat, Elite Headlight, Suspension Seatpost, and Cargo Package.

Electric trikes are a great choice for many riders, including seniors, people with mobility limitations, and those who need to carry heavy payloads. At $1,699, the Lectric XP Trike2 is an easy-to-ride, stable three-wheeler.

A 750-watt motor with 1,310 peak watts powers the XP Trike up to 17 mph and up to 70 miles of range on a charge. The Trike features a wide, soft seat with back support. Plus, it has a suspension seatpost and suspension fork for added comfort.

With a top speed of 28 mph, 81 miles of range, a 100mm-travel suspension fork, 27.5”x2.6”, a rack, and fenders, the Adventure Neo Allroad Speed’s name fits it to a T. This bike is built for adventures large and small, from commutes to work in the snow or rain, to gravel trails at your local park.

To power the Adventure, Cannondale uses a Bafang 750W rear hub motor and an easy-access 750 Wh removable battery. With its power and wide-range 8-speed drivetrain, you will get up every hill, while Tektro hydraulic disc brakes will control your speed on descents. Plus, it’s available in flashy red or more subdued matte black.

At $1,200, this Cannondale is 45% off its original price and is equipped with better parts than many lesser-known brands’ bikes priced hundreds more.

Many “step-through” e-bikes lack a truly low-step design, making them difficult for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, from REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. This makes the CTY a great choice for older riders, those with mobility limitations, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor; it provides smooth pedal assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem to custom-tune your riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for improved stopping power. For less than the cost of many unknown e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI’s warranty and service.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs. But don’t let the price fool you; this bike is value-packed. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Newton-meters of torque) and a 430-Watt-hour battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, it has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system on Pivot bikes), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain, four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the components of this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Electric bikes are great for commuting and city life. However, their added weight (sometimes as much as 90 or 100 pounds) can make e-bikes a pain to carry up flights of stairs, load onto a bus or train, or even move around in your garage.

Weighing only about 40 pounds, the Roadster v3 cuts weight without sacrificing much performance or adding cost. Ride1Up uses a 500 watt/50Nm rear hub motor with an internal battery for a clean, stealthy look. 700x45c gravel tires carry speed on pavement or hardpack dirt roads, and metal fenders keep the road spray off your clothes.

Electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and help you ride more of your favorite trails. We recommend full-suspension E-MTBs for aggressive and technical trails. But hardtails often work fine on easier trails and mellower terrain, and they cost a lot less than dual-suspension models.

Velotric keeps costs low on the Summit 1 by using a rear hub motor instead of a pricier mid-drive unit. The Summit also features an 8-speed Shimano drivetrain rather than more expensive 11- or 12-speed systems. However, Velotric gives the bike a 120mm thru-axle fork to soak up bumps, Shimano hydraulic disc brakes, and a full-color screen with Bluetooth connectivity.

Electric bikes are a great way for older riders to enjoy cycling and stay active. However, many commuter e-bikes have high top tubes, and even many step-through-style frames still require riders to swing their leg over the frame. The Velotric Discover has a Euro-style, low-step-through frame that makes it easier to get on and off.

Additional comfort features include an adjustable-rise stem, wide seat, and suspension seatpost. The Discover has a 28mph top speed and about 75 miles of range. At 63 pounds, it’s not super light, but it weighs less than many similarly priced e-bikes.

#8885. 8 Sugar-Free Electrolyte Powders That Don’t Suck

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix

When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

But the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate quickly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health issues (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition plan. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

The salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you plan to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

If you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is currently facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.)

With 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”

The flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

#8884. 6 Tips for Maintaining Your Fitness Routine During the Busy Holiday Season

Use these strategies to keep your training on track so you can start the new year feeling strong.

The holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide. Between shopping for gifts, attending holiday parties, and meeting work obligations, it can feel like there’s not enough time to squeeze in an hour-long workout session—so why even try?

Well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and New Year’s Day. A review published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021 suggests that you can reduce your workout time by two-thirds and still maintain your gains, as long as the intensity stays the same.

Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.

Setting an attainable goal for yourself, like running for at least 30 minutes two or three times per week, can make staying active through the holidays feel more doable. It’s how I was able to get back to exercise after a break, and it’s also how I plan to maintain my fitness this winter—in addition to following some of the best advice from my Runner’s World colleagues.

So ditch the all-or-nothing mindset and use the following tips to your advantage now, so when the New Year arrives, you’ll be ready to tackle your goals for 2027.

“I have a race in mid-January, so I am following a training plan [which keeps me motivated]. But I am also cross-training with step aerobics, and I’ve added jump training into my workouts. I was bored with my usual strength routine, so I decided to mix things up with kettlebell training, targeting my upper body and core.” —Donna Raskin, senior health and fitness editor

“I make time for new workout classes, like the ones offered by Solidcore and OrangeTheory to support my strength needs, because I usually don’t get to attend those sessions when I’m training for a race.” —Sara Hemstock, senior director of marketing and brand liaison

“I love doing strength work and some form of speed training in the winter. I recently found an indoor track in my local YMCA, and I’m excited to use that as an option for when it snows. There’s something nostalgic about it for me after running winter track as a kid.” —Kristine Kearns, associate health and fitness editor

“I love running on Christmas Day because it’s always so quiet in my hometown of Columbia, South Carolina. I usually run downtown, past the state capitol building, and through the University of South Carolina. The normally busy area turns into a complete ghost town! It’s a once-a-year experience and a personal tradition. I look forward to it every year.” —Theo Khaler, news editor

“Every year, I look forward to going home to North Carolina during the holidays because I get to test my fitness in my neighborhood Turkey Trot. It’s a community event put on by my high school, and it always draws a huge crowd.

The 5K race itself gives me something to look toward and train for in the fall. It’s a great chance to test my speed and have fun with the sport, but the best part has to be the community aspect. I catch up with old friends, teammates, coaches, teachers, and neighbors, and hearing about their own running journeys always fuels mine, too. Plus, each age-group winner wins a pie. Who doesn’t like free dessert?” —Ashley Tysiac, content hype editor

“I motivate myself by thinking of all the folks who decided not to run as I was bundled up, gutting out a sub-freezing effort. It just makes me feel proud thinking that I decided to lace up and get out the door that particular day when someone else may not have.

The thought process works both ways: If I decide to skip a cold-weather run, I think about all the people who are out there toughing it out while I’m sipping hot chocolate on my couch.” —Matt Rudisill, associate service editor

“This is the time of year when I try to add strength work into my routine because I am usually indoors at the gym more. But I find strength training so boring, so I experiment with different protein shakes to find the ones I really like, which keeps me motivated. I consider them a postworkout treat!” —Amanda Furrer, running reviews editor

“I treat myself to nice, new running clothes, and that makes cold weather running more enjoyable. I also like testing out new looks. It gives me something to look forward to.”—Hemstock

“Indoor workouts allow me to experiment with different outfits, like a shirt with comfortable sweatpants or oversized sweatsuits. That makes me feel really cozy and confident so I want to keep on training.” —Kearns

“I try to run at least a mile every day through the holidays, like a running streak. It can be inside or outside.” —Furrer

“I give myself permission to shorten any and all workouts. Even if I just commit to 20 minutes, I usually end up doing more, but knowing I can stop early breaks down the barrier to getting started.” —Mallory Creveling, deputy editor, health and fitness.

Monique LeBrun is a health and fitness editor who is based in Easton, Pennsylvania. She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. Monique is passionate about creating content that empowers runners to become the best versions of themselves. As an avid runner and parent, she loves spending time outdoors with her daughter, who often accompanies her on weekend runs as her personal mini run coach.

#8883. Is Your Body Fat Percentage Holding Back Your Cycling Goals? The Answer Depends on Your Age and Ambition.

Your body fat percentage is a tool, not a judgment. Here’s are the recommended ranges that cyclists can use to support their goals.

For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s important to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.)

🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

There isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

While the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

It’s important to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

However, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

When it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

As an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

Understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

Natascha is an editor and writer covering health, fitness, and the ways people move through the world. She’s been a NASM-certified personal trainer for more than a decade, with a background in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She has additional CES, CNC, BCS, and SFC certifications. She is also a level-2 certified Spinning instructor. Her work has appeared in Bicycling, Runner’s World, and other outlets, and her experience spans both editorial and hands-on work across the fitness industry. Whether she’s writing about training, health, or performance, she’s most interested in making complicated topics useful, approachable, and helpful. She is currently the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health.

#8882. Both Men and Women Are Quitting Running Because of Undiagnosed Pelvic Floor Problems. Experts Want to Break the Taboo So More Runners Can Get Help.

This underappreciated powerhouse is the secret to great running. But many of us don’t know how to care for it, and put up with pain, discomfort, even leakage. Here’s why it happens and what you can do about it before it derails your progress.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 issue of Runner’s World.

“What fresh hell is this?” Liz B. wondered during a four-mile run on a chilly December night five months after giving birth. She was 2.7 miles into an out-and-back route when she realized she’d leaked a little urine. “It happened on and off the rest of the way home,” says the 36-year-old from central Ohio, who prefers not to use her full name when talking about urinary incontinence, which affects 25 million adult Americans.

This was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life. Liz, a physical therapist who works with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury patients, had been a runner for nearly her whole life. Her father, who just ran his 91st marathon at the age of 77, had taken her out for jogs when she was a toddler, and she was hooked on long distances ever since. Her idea of a “good time” was waking up at 5 a.m. on a Saturday to go for a scenic 16-mile run with her sister. Before becoming a mom, she’d run eight marathons and was eight minutes shy of qualifying for Boston. “I had always been excited to get pregnant and had dreams of pushing my kid in a running stroller.” But her regular runs came to a screeching halt 19 weeks into her pregnancy when she developed peripheral blood clots and had to reduce physical activity because of the pain. She’d been looking forward to lacing up her running shoes again, but after a difficult labor, she developed pelvic organ prolapse, a condition where weak muscles allow one or more pelvic organs (like the uterus or bladder) to drop down onto other organs or out of the vagina.

Liz had been working with a pelvic floor therapist to treat the prolapse and had just spent the previous six weeks easing back into running. But she was frustrated with the slow progress in coming back to her pre-pregnancy eight-minute mile. “Once I had my baby, my pace slowed to a 10:30 mile,” Liz says. “And if I ran under a 9:00, I’d pee my pants a little.”

Pelvic floor dysfunction, an inability to coordinate pelvic floor muscles, is more prevalent than most of us realize. Research shows that approximately 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will experience pelvic floor dysfunction in their lifetime—and that’s just what gets reported. Particularly in women, hormonal fluctuations, added weight, and the strain of pregnancy and childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.

As much as we dislike the fact, high-impact physical activity—like running—can exacerbate these issues. That’s because as you run, your pelvic floor repeatedly absorbs impact and dampens vibrations, says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT, a physical therapist in Los Angeles who specializes in returning women to fitness after injury and pregnancy.

“Running creates an added challenge to your pelvic floor beyond the movements of everyday activities,” explains Carrie Pagliano, PT, a pelvic floor specialist based in Arlington, Virginia. “It puts greater impact and pressure on your musculoskeletal system.”

The good news is these issues can be resolved. But too often, they go undiagnosed. For one thing, there’s the stigma. Talking about pelvic floor issues can feel taboo because we’ve been conditioned to have shame around that area of the body. What’s more, most of us aren’t even sure where our pelvic floor is, what it does, or how it can become dysfunctional. But pelvic floor muscles are like any other muscles in your body. “They need training, they need relaxation, they need strengthening, and they need attention,” says Sara Reardon, DPT, WCS, a board-certified pelvic floor physical therapist in New Orleans. And finally, we need to stop accepting pelvic floor issues as normal. “When we normalize pelvic floor conditions, they don’t get treated,” says Reardon. “Pelvic floor problems are common, but not normal, and it’s the conversations about them that need to be normal.”

Here’s what you need to know to keep your pelvic floor in shape and your running on track.

Your pelvic floor consists of a group of muscles going from your pubic bone, which is located just below your abdomen, to your tailbone, which is at the bottom of your spine. It holds and protects the bladder, urethra, vagina, prostate, bowel, rectum, and anus. Were you able to “hold it” until you got to the bathroom? That’s your pelvic floor on the job. Couldn’t wait until you reached home and had to go immediately behind a tree or a parked car? Your pelvic floor may have clocked out. Got an erection? That’s in part thanks to your pelvic floor. Had a vaginal birth? Your pelvic floor was working triple overtime. Had a great orgasm? Yup, it chimes in there too.

When you think about pelvic floor issues, urinary incontinence likely comes to mind first. In one small study, approximately 46 percent of elite female endurance runners and cross-country skiers reported leaking urine when sneezing or coughing. But urinary incontinence is just one type of pelvic floor disorder—and it’s actually least likely to make a runner seek medical help. “They’re worried they’ll be told to stop running,” Pagliano says. More often, what draws runners with pelvic problems into an expert’s office are other symptoms: not being able to urinate or defecate, having sharp or nagging pelvic pain, pelvic organ prolapse, or fecal incontinence.

Despite its importance, the pelvic floor is under-researched. “The truth is we’ve never cared about pelvic health as a society,” says Wiebe. It’s been seen as a primarily women’s issue, and historically women are underrepresented in medical research. And because pelvic floor issues are mainly linked to postpartum health, men tend to be left out of the conversation as well; experts are only beginning to understand the impact it has on men.

An hour after Gordon Garner wrapped up the perfect 20-mile training run, he called his wife to let her know he was driving himself to the emergency room.

Over the previous year, the then 38-year-old software development manager had been transforming into a runner. He worked his way up from doing a Couch to 5K to prepping for his first marathon. Everything about this long run had gone according to plan: He ran at his goal pace for the upcoming 26.2 miles he wanted to complete in under four hours; he stopped every six miles to hydrate; and he felt so good, he was tempted to keep running. “Stick to the training plan,” Garner told himself, as he wrapped his last mile and headed back to his Dallas home. Before he hopped in the shower, he felt the need to pee but couldn’t. After he washed up, he tried again, and only a few drops came out. The pain was excruciating.

The ER doctors quickly ruled out kidney stones, which Garner feared were causing the pain. To empty his bladder, they had to catheterize him. “I have a pretty high pain tolerance,” says Garner, who once broke both wrists playing basketball and an elbow falling from a bike. “I was in a world of pain when they put the catheter in.” Unable to determine what was going on, the hospital discharged him.

But Garner still didn’t know what was wrong and whether it would happen again—which it did at mile 12 of the marathon he was training for. Once more, he felt the urge to pee, so he stopped at the public restroom, and nothing would come out. He kept running for six more miles before dropping out.

Ultimately, it would take two misdiagnoses, three prescriptions that didn’t resolve the issue, and several more practitioner appointments until he finally found an answer from a physical therapist. “I know exactly what’s happening to you,” Garner remembers her telling him. She explained that the muscles of Garner’s pelvic floor were continuously contracting and wouldn’t relax. The correct diagnosis was a dysfunction known as hypertonic pelvic floor.

For years, the main conversation around pelvic floor problems has focused on strengthening weakness through Kegel exercises. And yet that wasn’t the case for Garner, nor is it for many others. The pelvic floor is a complex system of muscles that needs to not only contract, squeeze, and lift, but also relax and release. “Your pelvic floor can be plenty strong but not meeting the demands that are being placed on it because it’s not behaving the way you need it to,” Wiebe says. If your pelvic floor is constantly contracting, it’s clearly strong, but it can’t perform any other function at the same time.

But the relationship is not as simple as a weak pelvic floor causing leakage or a strong one leading to retention. A 2021 meta-analysis published in Cureus Medical Journal concluded that even a strong pelvic floor can lead to urinary incontinence. In fact, some young female runners who have never given birth (a life event usually linked to incontinence) can experience urine leakage. “We also have studies showing pelvic floor activation is similar between incontinent and continent runners, so the status of the pelvic floor muscles can’t be the only cause of leakage,” says Wiebe.

Experts like Wiebe consider how your pelvic floor behaves over time—not in just one moment. “If someone doesn’t leak while doing all their regular daily activities, but then leaks at the very end of a 45-minute run, that pelvic floor is pretty strong, but it may not have the endurance for a long run,” Wiebe says. “And if that person only ran 35 or 40 minutes, they might never experience running-related incontinence. Endurance is different from strength and may better explain leaks for some.”

There is more to pelvic floors than just tightening and relaxing. “A lot of people think the pelvic floor is like a light switch: It’s either on or off,” Pagliano says. “In reality, it’s more of a dimmer switch because it has to…transition from very bright to dim or from high to low very quickly, like when we’re running.” In your body, that transition looks like your pelvic floor muscles lengthening, shortening, and working more or less to match activity demand with every foot strike.

And the pelvic floor doesn’t act in isolation. “If I have a patient whose balance is off and they don’t have the ability to navigate impact as well through their ankle, knee, and hip, then there’s more work to manage impact that gets kicked up to the pelvic floor,” says Pagliano. “I often joke that the pelvic floor is like the mom of the body. If other muscles are just like, ‘Oh, I don’t want to do that,’ then the pelvic floor has to step up and do it.”

Colleen Quigley has spent the past five years crisscrossing the globe trying to relieve a nagging source of pain that often prevented her from performing her best. “I had recurring injuries in my left foot, but a lot of the time pain would also show up in my lower back or my hip,” Quigley says. “At a certain point, I wasn’t able to train at a high level anymore.” The steeplechase specialist, NCAA champion, and current world-record holder in the 4 x 1500m relay saw more than 50 different experts, flying at one point to Germany for injections into her back.

Then one practitioner noticed a particular problem. “He muscle-tested me for things that were going on in my pelvis, then he showed me an exercise to relieve tension and tested me again,” says the 2016 Olympian. “Suddenly all the problems I tested for in my pelvis disappeared.” The exercise? A tongue stretch to relieve tightness in her jaw. “Jaw tension and pelvic floor tension have a relationship,” Wiebe says. “It’s essentially both ends of the alimentary tract.”

It was a revelation to Quigley and struck a chord with other runners. Quigley’s Instagram video demonstrating the stretch she now uses as part of her warmup routine to help relax her pelvis has gathered more than 42,000 likes. Although a single change wasn’t the solution to all of Quigley’s injuries, the jaw-pelvis connection helped resolve some symptoms that doctors couldn’t explain.

Quigley’s experience illustrates shortcomings in how diagnoses are sometimes made. Doctors and patients often focus on symptoms instead of looking for the root cause. In one study, researchers in Canada screened women who came to an orthopedic clinic for lower back and pelvic pain for pelvic floor muscle dysfunction. The study found that 95 percent of the women with lumbopelvic pain also had underlying pelvic floor dysfunction that needed to be addressed.

And Quigley’s hip pain was likely related to her pelvic issues as well. “We have deep hip stability muscles that are part of our pelvic floor,” explains Reardon. “When people start experiencing a high hamstring strain or they have a deep hip pain they feel like they just can’t get to, that can be often pelvic-floor-related.” And it doesn’t stop there. Reardon says that pain from pelvic floor dysfunction can show up in various and unexpected ways, including during bowel movements and even intercourse, which is why it’s important to find an expert with experience treating these issues (see sidebar).

Fortunately, the conversation around pelvic floor issues is evolving. “We’re starting to see patterns that might explain why you and I might have the same symptoms but maybe have different ways that we find resolutions,” says Pagliano. For runners, it might be a matter of your stride, your form, or even your breathing. “If someone holds their abdomen tight while they are running or are constantly holding their breath during normal everyday activities, we often see pelvic floor muscles that have higher tone or activity and actually don’t relax when they should. Sometimes this leads to leakage with running. Just strengthening the pelvic floor below won’t matter if those muscles are already ‘on’ and have lost the ability to contract and relax.”

As for Gordon Garner, after finally finding the right therapist, he scaled back his running for a few weeks while working on stretching and breath-control exercises. In 2023, he ran 40 miles in a 24-hour period to celebrate his 40th birthday. “I was a little worried, just because I was testing these new boundaries, but with my exercises and my breathing techniques, I had no issues. I’m very in touch with my pelvic floor muscles now.”

Liz finally found a therapist who helped her establish a strength-training routine in order to coordinate pelvic floor muscles again, pay attention to her body’s signals, and get back to running. Twenty months after giving birth, she raced her ninth marathon, without having to worry about leaking midrun. When your pelvic floor isn’t functioning as it should, “you realize that everything you do—breathing, talking, laughing, moving, carrying things—everything involves the pelvic floor,” Liz says.

With the right help and a better understanding of your body, pelvic floor problems can be solved. It’s a commitment, but your running will thank you. “Clients will always say, ‘Do I have to do these exercises forever?’” says Reardon. “I tell them, ‘Yes, to some extent, if you’re going to keep running.’”

Lauren Garges, DPT, director of pelvic rehab with St. Luke’s University Health Network in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, shares a simple at-home test that can help determine if you’re suffering from an overactive pelvic floor:

• Sit on a large stability ball or a rolled-up hand towel. There should be pressure on the perineum, the space between the genitals and anus.

• Using the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or gas, imagine you’re trying to vacuum up a marble. Then, actively try to relax those muscles to see if they go back down, like an elevator.

“If they’re too tight, nothing may happen because your muscles are already as tight as they can get,” she says. “Or you might be able to squeeze upward but cannot feel the downward [release]. That’s a sign of tension.”

If you find contracting the muscles challenging, Garges says, it’s a sign of pelvic floor weakness.

Before you start doing kegels—especially if you have incontinence or other pelvic floor problems—see a pelvic floor therapist to ensure it makes sense to add them to your routine, as they’re not for everyone, says Nora Arnold, DPT, a pelvic health physical therapist with Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. If you get the go-ahead, Arnold offers these cues for correct form:

• It’s best to get the hang of it lying down and then progressing to adding in practice sitting and standing.

• Squeeze your pelvic floor like you’re holding back from passing gas.

• Contract as if you’re stopping the flow of urine (but don’t do this while you’re actually peeing, as it could result in bladder infection).

• Draw your pubic bone and tailbone toward one another.

• Contract as if you are drawing your sit bones together.

• Pull your pelvic floor up as if lifting your bladder toward your heart.

• You need to both squeeze and lift—people forget that second part. Make sure to fully relax the pelvic floor muscles between reps. Breathe through each contraction and relaxation.

• The number of repetitions is best decided by a PT; however, a good place to start is 3x10 contractions, holding for 10 seconds while breathing.

This deep breathing trains coordination between the pelvic floor and the diaphragm. When your diaphragm engages fully, it encourages your pelvic floor to relax and lengthen, Arnold says.

• To start, lie on your back. You can also do this in child’s pose, happy baby pose, a deep squat, or reclined sitting.

• Breathe in through your nose for four counts. Let your breath be as slow and full as possible. Your pelvic floor should relax and lengthen passively, just like your belly.

• Exhale through your mouth for six counts.

• For maximum benefit, try to incorporate this into your routine for five to 10 minutes a day. But even just 10 repetitions can make a difference.

Check experience / “As a runner, one of the most valuable things you can do is look for a pelvic floor therapist who knows sports medicine and pelvic health,” says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT. If you’re postpartum, you might also seek out someone who has worked with moms; and if you’re male, you might look for a therapist who has experience with male clients. You can find a list of providers through the American Physical Therapy Association. Read online reviews to see what other patient experiences were like.

Consider a virtual visit / While some therapy sessions may need to be done in person, many can be done remotely. If there isn’t a great pelvic floor specialist in your area, try working with a therapist online. “I’ve been doing telehealth since before COVID-19,” says Carrie Pagliano, PT. “If I can get a really good sense of why you’re having symptoms by the questions that I ask, you can get resolution. The key is getting the right ‘why.’ After that, the ‘how’ is easy.” Make sure to offer details about whether you were a bedwetter as a child, your birthing history, or when you experience pelvic floor problems, for example.

Don’t stop until you find the right one / Garner, Quigley, and Liz all had to reach out to multiple practitioners before they found the right person. “You don’t try on one pair of pants, say they didn’t fit, and then never wear pants again,” says Reardon. “You have to keep trying different medical professionals until you find the right one.”

As the former health director at Family Circle magazine, Lynya developed content to improve the well-being of its 18 million readers. She’s worked as an editor at Glamour, Essence, Seventeen, Heart & Soul, Parenting and more. She also co-edited ESSENCE’s The Black Woman’s Guide To Healthy Living. She received her B.A. in English from Harvard University, integrative health training at Duke, and plenty of life lessons in her hometown of New York City.

Picture this: you settle into a fully flat bed at 35,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, the city lights of New York fading behind you. In seven hours, you'll be in Paris. But right now, in this seat — a seat that costs upward of $6,000 in cash — you paid 53,000 points to be here. That's the Air France Business Class experience on the JFK–CDG route, and it's one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions available to the ChooseFI community today. Let's talk about the math, because the math is what makes this a genuine FI moment. A round-trip business class ticket between New York and Paris on Air France routinely retails for $3,000 on the low end and climbs to $6,000 or beyond during peak travel periods. At 53,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, you're looking at a value of **5.7 to 11.3 cents per point** — in a world where most points are considered excellent at 1.5 to 2 cents. You are, quite literally, squeezing 3 to 7 times the average value out of every mile you've earned. The pricing inefficiency here is real and it's structural. Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program releases discounted award seats monthly, sometimes cutting standard pricing by 25–50%. When a Promo Reward surfaces on a transatlantic business class route, the gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you pay in miles becomes almost absurd. A $4,000 cash ticket redeemable for 53,000 points you transferred at no cost from your Chase Sapphire Reserve? That's **7.5 cents per point** — money that your future self will thank you for. Beyond the numbers is the *experience* itself. Air France's long-haul business class product on the Boeing 777-300ER features a fully flat bed in a 1-2-1 configuration, direct aisle access from every seat, genuine French hospitality, and a meal service that feels like a restaurant, not an afterthought. This isn't a product you suffer through — it's one you savor. For a community that builds wealth intentionally so they can live fully, this is exactly what travel rewards are designed to unlock: a world-class experience at a fraction of the cost, because you understood the system.

Monthly promotional pricing makes premium European travel consistently accessible

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

Let's walk through a real-world example that illustrates exactly why the ChooseFI community gets excited about this redemption.

The Booking: You're flying JFK → CDG in Air France Business Class on a Boeing 777-300ER. It's a Tuesday evening departure — one of the best days for award availability — and you've snagged a Promo Reward seat at 53,000 Flying Blue miles plus approximately $65 in government taxes.

The Cash Alternative: A quick search on Google Flights shows the same seat retailing for $4,200 on that date. That's not an anomaly — transatlantic business class averages $3,000–$6,000 depending on season and advance purchase. At $4,200 in cash versus 53,000 miles, you're extracting 7.9 cents per point in value. Your Chase Ultimate Rewards points just became extraordinarily potent.

The Experience: You arrive at JFK and head to the Air France lounge before departure — accessible as a business class passenger. From the moment you board, the difference from economy is visceral. Your seat in the 1-2-1 configuration means no climbing over a stranger; you have direct aisle access. The seat fully reclines into a 180-degree flat bed with a thick mattress pad and proper bedding — not a glorified recliner, an actual bed. The meal service begins shortly after departure: a starter, a main course with real silverware, a cheese course, dessert, and a selection of French wines that would be at home in a Parisian bistro.

Seven hours later, you land at CDG having slept properly, eaten well, and arrived ready to explore Paris instead of recovering from an overnight in a middle seat. You step off the plane into Terminal 2E, collect your bags, and you're in the city within an hour.

The FI Math: Those 53,000 points came from everyday spending on your Chase Sapphire Reserve — grocery runs, gas, a few restaurant meals over the course of six months. You didn't buy the points. You earned them on purchases you were already making, transferred them in minutes, and unlocked a $4,200 experience for $65 out of pocket. That's the ChooseFI travel rewards system working exactly as designed.

Do this: Set a recurring monthly calendar reminder for Promo Rewards. Promo Rewards drop in the first week of each month and popular routes sell out fast. The readers who consistently land these redemptions aren't lucky — they're systematic. Mark the first Monday of every month as your "check Flying Blue" day.

Do this: Use an open-jaw routing to maximize your Europe trip. Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into one city and out of another within a single award booking. Fly JFK → CDG, travel through France, and fly home from AMS → JFK. You've just built a multi-city trip without paying for positioning flights — and used a single 53,000-mile award to do it.

Do this: Transfer points only after confirming availability. This cannot be overstated. Transfers from Chase and Amex are instant, but they are also irreversible. Never initiate a transfer until you have confirmed, with your own eyes, that the award seat is available and bookable. The five-minute shortcut of transferring first has stranded miles in countless accounts.

Avoid this: Booking standard dynamic awards without checking Promo Rewards first. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing on standard awards can be significantly higher than Promo Reward pricing — sometimes 30–50% more miles for the exact same seat. Always check if the month's Promo Rewards include your route before defaulting to a standard award.

Avoid this: Ignoring the surcharge line item. On standard (non-Promo) Flying Blue awards for Air France flights, carrier surcharges can add $200–$500 to your out-of-pocket cost. This doesn't eliminate the value, but it changes the math. Always review the full fee breakdown before confirming. Promo Rewards typically waive these surcharges — another reason to prioritize them.

Do this: Stack earning across multiple cards. You don't need to earn 53,000 points on a single card. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to Flying Blue at 1:1. Accumulate across programs, then choose the best transfer source when a Promo Reward surfaces. This flexibility is a structural advantage of the ChooseFI approach to travel rewards.

Know your expiry window. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one transaction (even a small earning or redemption) every two years to protect your balance.

This redemption is built for the intentional traveler — someone who has spent time accumulating points on one or more major transferable currencies and is ready to deploy them strategically rather than cash them in for coffee and Amazon gift cards.

Minimum requirements: You'll want at least 53,000 points in a single transferable currency (Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt) or the ability to combine balances to reach that threshold. No Flying Blue status is required — this is available to any member.

This redemption is rated **moderate**, and that's an honest assessment. The experience itself — transferring points, booking on FlyingBlue.com — is straightforward. What adds complexity is the timing and strategy layer. **What makes it moderately challenging:** 1. **Promo Rewards require patience and timing.** The best pricing surfaces once a month, for specific routes, in limited quantities. You can't always book exactly when you want to travel. The reader who succeeds here is the one who monitors monthly releases and has flexible travel dates — or is willing to book 6–9 months in advance when a Promo Reward aligns with their plans. 2. **Dynamic pricing creates uncertainty.** Unlike programs with fixed award charts, Flying Blue's standard pricing varies. Without a Promo Reward, your 53,000-mile sweet spot may price higher. This makes pre-transfer research non-negotiable. 3. **Points accumulation across multiple programs requires organization.** The good news: every major transferable currency transfers to Flying Blue at 1:1. The challenge: knowing which account holds what, and when to move miles. **Three tips to make this easier:** - **Use the 359-day booking window.** Flying Blue opens awards 359 days in advance. For popular summer routes, start checking Promo Rewards at month-eight to month-ten before your trip. - **Follow community resources.** The ChooseFI community and frequent flyer forums will alert you when a strong Promo Reward drops — you don't have to monitor alone. - **Practice the search before you need it.** Log into FlyingBlue.com today and run a practice award search. Get comfortable with the interface before you're racing to book a Promo Reward seat. If you can earn miles and check a website once a month, you can execute this redemption. Thousands of travelers in the ChooseFI community have done it — you're next.

Major US-to-Europe routes like JFK-CDG or JFK-AMS tend to appear on the Promo Rewards list every 2-4 months. Less popular routes may appear less frequently. The key is consistent monthly monitoring so you catch the promotion when it appears for your target destination.

Flying Blue does not offer formal stopover benefits on award tickets. However, you can book a one-way promo award to your gateway city and then add a separate low-cost carrier or train connection to your final destination. Many travelers use this strategy to explore Paris or Amsterdam for a few days before continuing onward.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

Both airlines offer lie-flat business class seats with direct aisle access on long-haul aircraft. Air France's cabin tends to emphasize French culinary presentation and wine service, while KLM has a more understated Dutch design aesthetic. Both are solid products. When booking through Flying Blue, you can choose either airline based on routing, schedule, or cabin preference.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards turn business class to Europe from a special-occasion splurge into a repeatable system. By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. The fuel surcharges are a real cost to factor in, but even with that overhead, promo business class awards deliver 5-12 cents per mile in value. Set the monthly reminder and let the system work.

#8880. I Dug Through the Early Black Friday Cycling Sales—Here’s the Gear Actually Worth Buying Before Winter Hits

Upgrade your winter rides with deals on cycling gloves, trainers, helmets, tires, lights, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Fall riding season is coming to a close, and winter is right around the corner. While late fall and winter mean shorter daylight hours for riding, it’s a great time to save on cycling gear—for yourself or if shopping early for holiday gifts. Many brands are discounting old inventory at great prices, and others are clearing room for new gear hitting shelves after the New Year.

Although many of the best holiday sales aren’t until Black Friday and Cyber Monday, some retailers are running Early Black Friday promotions with big deals and discounts on top-rated gear. In addition to Pre-Black Friday sales, Amazon, REI, bike brands, and other retailers are offering deep discounts on cycling equipment, components, apparel, and accessories you need for road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.

Pre-Black Friday sales are a great chance to stock up on frequently used consumables—such as tubes, tire sealant, chain lube, and nutrition products—and to grab the gear you need for late-fall and winter rides. They’re also a great way to save money on usually pricey riding apparel: If you’ve been holding out on buying a new vest, arm warmers, jerseys, a jacket, or even shoes, some brands are offering deep discounts on cycling clothing and accessories.

Below are sales and deals hubs for several top online cycling gear and bike retailers, plus links to sales from leading clothing brands and bike companies. These are some of the best deals on editor-tested gear we’ve spotted so far. Bookmark this page and return for updates as even more deals come online.
